title: Gist tokens replace old context; raw chunks re-expand from flash
idea: Box: summarize × agent runtime × document chunk × leaves recent window × raw tokens on SSD. Older chunks are replaced by a few learned gist tokens' KV; if attention to a gist crosses a threshold the runtime re-prefills the original chunk from flash (zoom-in).
why: Million-token agents carry enormous KV; gist plus zoom keeps it ~20× smaller with recoverable fidelity.

title: Multimode-fiber speckle hashing finds duplicate pages for free
idea: A multimode glass fiber is a fixed random matrix, so the speckle pattern at its output is a random projection of its input, which is a locality-sensitive hash. Modulate candidate pages or KV chunks onto a laser, send them through the fiber and read a 1-kpixel camera; matching speckle signatures flag exact and near-duplicate content for merging.
why: Background dedup scanning at near-zero silicon cost and energy, including near-duplicate merging (images, KV chunks, embedding rows) that exact hashing misses: 10-30% smaller footprint on VM-dense and serving hosts.

title: Solera optimizer: staggered moment updates live in persistent flash
idea: Like a sherry solera where only a fraction of each barrel is drawn and topped up per cycle, keep Adam's first and second moments in persistent CXL flash and update only a rotating 1/k slice per step (the rest use slightly stale moments), bounding NV write rate and wear while weights stay in HBM.
why: Optimizer state is 2-3x weight size in training; moves it to durable cheap media and doubles as continuous checkpointing.

title: Skyrmion reservoir replaces recurrent weights with magnetic dynamics
idea: Input currents excite a Ta/CoFeB/MgO skyrmion fabric whose nonlinear, fading-memory dynamics act as the state transition of a sequence model. A few MTJs read out the state, so only a small linear readout is stored, not large recurrent or state-space matrices.
why: Removes most weight storage from streaming time-series models (sensor fusion, keyword spotting), with 10-100x fewer stored parameters.

title: Predictive-coding memory storing only residuals of a tiny predictor
idea: A small fixed predictor (linear or tiny neural) in the memory controller predicts each 64 B line from its neighbors and a per-page context on every access. DRAM stores only the entropy-coded residuals. This is the brain's and video codecs' predictive coding, run at the nanosecond scale.
why: Structured data (tables, pointers, tensors) leaves small residuals, for 1.5-2.5x capacity beyond pattern-based compression.

title: Phylogenetic tree storage for resident model variants
idea: All fine-tuned variants resident on a node form an evolutionary tree. Each node stores 1-bit sign deltas plus per-channel scales relative to its parent, rebuilt on the fly in the GEMM epilogue. Serving 100 variants costs about one base model plus 100 x 1/16 of its size.
why: Multi-tenant serving memory falls 10-30x compared with separate copies. This extends LoRA-style sharing to full fine-tunes.

title: Swap DRAM KV cache for an append-only log on write-once NVM
idea: Substitute DRAM with endurance-limited NVM by matching the workload: KV entries are written once and read thousands of times, so an HBM-style stack of dense PCM/RRAM dies holds them as an append-only log. The accelerator prefetches the next layer's KV into SRAM while the current layer computes, which hides the ~100-300 ns NVM reads. A conversation's whole region is erased at once when it ends, so each cell sees only ~1e5-1e6 writes in its lifetime.
why: KV cache is 30-70% of HBM demand in long-context serving. The write-once pattern sidesteps NVM's endurance limit, so 2-3x fewer DRAM bits are needed per served token.

title: Cell SPE local stores, fixed: compiler-scheduled flash-to-SRAM layer streaming
idea: Cell's SPEs died because programmers hand-wrote double-buffered DMA into 256 KB local stores. Transformer inference is a fully static dataflow, so the compiler generates the DMA schedule: stream layer N+1 weights from NVMe flash into SRAM while layer N computes, picking batch size so compute time covers flash read time.
why: DRAM-free throughput inference servers with only SRAM and flash, removing multi-GB DRAM per accelerator.

title: Neural generative codec memory with residual correction
idea: Worsen: store every structured dataset verbatim in DRAM. Flip: train a per-dataset generative model and store only its weights plus a small entropy-coded residual; an accelerator in the memory path reconstructs requested records exactly by running the model and adding the residual.
why: Cost: 30-300x effective GB per physical GB for logs, telemetry, tabular and embedding data; trades decode energy and latency.

title: Eliminate unused high bits with profile-guided field narrowing
idea: An LLVM plugin records observed value ranges of struct fields in production profiles, then shrinks int64 fields to 8/16/32 bits, bit-packs booleans and reorders fields to remove padding, with trap-on-overflow guards.
why: C/C++/Rust service heaps shrink 10-25% with a recompile.

title: Optane App Direct, fixed: read-only weights served from NAND
idea: Optane persistent memory died partly on crash-consistency programming complexity and write wear. Sidestep both by exposing only immutable data: a CXL controller maps SLC NAND as read-only load/store memory, caches 256 B sectors in the NAND dies' own page-buffer latches, and serves model weights and embedding tables with no DRAM buffer.
why: Read-mostly data moves to ~10x cheaper-per-bit NAND, and no persistence-semantics or endurance problem remains.

title: Shadow router prefetches next-layer MoE experts from CXL flash
idea: Box: tiering × MoE inference runtime × expert × predicted one layer early × CXL-attached low-latency NAND. A tiny predictor maps the current hidden state to the next layer's likely experts, which stream into a small HBM expert cache while the current layer computes.
why: MoE models leave >90% of parameters idle per token; holding only active plus predicted experts shrinks resident weights 4–8×.

title: Compress before encrypt with type-tagged controller codecs
idea: Worsen: encrypt memory first so every byte looks random and nothing compresses. Flip: put a compression stage ahead of the memory-encryption engine, choosing a codec per page type tag (float-exponent, pointer-delta, small-int, text) and storing ciphertext of the compressed line.
why: Capacity: restores 1.5-2.5x compression on confidential-computing VMs that currently get none.

title: Eliminate fragmentation slack with transparent hardware object compaction
idea: The memory controller keeps a small redirection table and relocates live small objects in the background into dense pages, updating mappings like a hardware copying collector, so malloc arenas stop wasting free holes.
why: Long-running allocators waste 15-30% of DRAM to fragmentation; reclaiming it is pure capacity gain without app changes.

title: Acousto-optic steered holographic cube as microsecond tier below DRAM
idea: A TeO2 acousto-optic deflector steers a laser to any of ~10^5 page holograms in a photopolymer cube within ~5 us. Each flash reads a 1 Mb page onto a camera chip. Cold but randomly accessed data, such as embedding tables and old KV, lives here instead of DRAM.
why: A dense, cheap page tier between DRAM and SSD lets DRAM shrink 30-50% in embedding-heavy workloads.

title: Minify integer widths with compiler value-range struct shrinking
idea: Minify data layouts at compile time: whole-program value-range analysis narrows fields (64 to 16 bits where provable), reorders fields to remove padding and packs booleans into bitfields. A guarded overflow trap re-widens a type at runtime if a profile was wrong.
why: Typical C++/Rust server heaps shrink ~1.2-1.8x with zero hardware change.

title: Game procedural generation: regenerate pseudorandom tensors from seeds
idea: Borrowed from seed-generated game worlds: any tensor that is pseudorandom by construction (random-feature projections, frozen random bases, sketch hash tables, dropout masks) is stored as a 64-bit seed and regenerated on demand by a counter-based Philox unit beside the tensor core. Models are trained with seeded frozen bases so only small learned coefficients are stored.
why: Turns GBs of stored randomness into bytes; for seeded-basis models, claims 5-20x less weight DRAM at the cost of cheap on-die generation.

title: Library card catalogs: SRAM filters front non-volatile records
idea: Borrowed from libraries that keep a compact card catalog by the door and books in the stacks: large DRAM hash tables (dedup indexes, key-value stores, routing tables) are replaced by SRAM-resident ribbon/cuckoo filters plus learned position models that point to the exact NVM block, so each lookup costs one NVM read.
why: Index structures often dominate server DRAM; filters need ~1-2 bytes per key versus 30-100 in DRAM tables, a 20-50x reduction with no refresh.

title: Seed-regenerated tensors replace stored random matrices
idea: TRIZ #26 Copying: replace stored pseudo-random data (random projections, sketch matrices, hash tables, dropout masks, random-feature kernels) by a seed plus a counter-based PRNG (Philox-style) unit near memory that regenerates any element on access, a perfect copy that costs no bits.
why: Sketching and random-projection-heavy models can hold GBs of pseudo-random tensors; removes that slice entirely at small compute cost.

title: Learned indexes replace in-memory hash tables and B-trees
idea: Inverts 'an index stores keys and pointers': piecewise-linear models predict a key's position in a sorted array to within a small error window, replacing in-memory B-trees and hash indexes. Software only, on any existing CPU.
why: Index memory falls 10-100x for large key-value stores and databases, where indexes are often 20-40% of DRAM.

title: Hash joins without hash tables: in-bank PIM probe units
idea: Po: the CPU lives inside the RAM. Compare-and-gather units beside each DRAM bank scan the build-side relation in place and stream out only matching tuple IDs, so analytical joins and group-bys never materialize multi-GB hash tables in main memory.
why: Intermediate hash tables can be 1-3x input size in analytics; in-bank probing removes them and cuts data-movement energy (facts 5, 8).

title: Octopus arms think locally: filtering engines inside CXL memory modules
idea: Two-thirds of an octopus's neurons sit in its arms. Each CXL memory module gets a small engine for scan, filter, hash-probe and gather, so analytics and database operators run where the data sits and return only results. That eliminates the host-side staging buffers, decoded copies and hash tables that currently mirror the data in local DRAM.
why: Analytics nodes often hold 2-3 copies of hot data (raw, decoded and intermediate). Near-data operators cut host DRAM 30-60% and also cut data-movement energy.

title: Selenium trace: SRAM sketches replace DRAM hash tables until certain
idea: Selenium is essential in trace amounts; big DRAM hash tables for counting, dedup, joins and membership are replaced by SRAM-resident sketches (count-min, HyperLogLog, cuckoo filters) that answer most queries, and the exact table, kept compressed in DRAM or flash, is consulted only on sketch-positive or close-call results.
why: Sketches are 10-100x smaller than exact tables and SRAM costs ~50x less energy per bit than DRAM, so typical lookups fall >10x in energy and the index footprint in DRAM shrinks sharply (energy, density).

title: Dispersive SAW chirp lines compress radar data before the ADC
idea: Automotive radars buffer the full range-Doppler cube in DRAM. Instead, an AlN-on-sapphire dispersive SAW delay line does analog pulse compression and range transformation on each chirp, so only range bins above the CFAR threshold are digitized and stored. SAW devices are already qualified to AEC-Q200 at 125 C, and the piezo material is stable far beyond that.
why: Cuts radar DRAM buffering 10-30x and saves ADC power, freeing DRAM in ADAS domain controllers.

title: Plated-wire NDRO memory for read-mostly tensors
idea: Revive Apollo-era plated wire: electroplate a 1 um NiFe film with circumferential anisotropy around lithographed copper lines, cross them with word straps, and read non-destructively by sensing the small magnetization tilt a word pulse causes, writing with coincident word and bit currents. Every step is UV litho, sputtering and plating.
why: Non-destructive readout means no restore cycle and no page overfetch (fact 8); a nonvolatile, unlimited-read tier for weights and embeddings moves read-mostly data off DRAM at zero standby power.

title: Vector fonts replace bitmaps: neural hash fields for embedding tables
idea: Borrowed from type foundries' switch from bitmap to outline fonts: recommendation and vocabulary embedding tables (100 GB-10 TB) are replaced by a multi-resolution hash grid plus a tiny MLP decoder (Instant-NGP style) that renders an ID's embedding on demand, with hot IDs memoized in a small cache.
why: Embedding tables are the largest DRAM consumers in ad/recommendation fleets; 10-100x capacity reduction by trading capacity for cheap FLOPs.

title: IBM MXT, fixed: compression moved behind CXL where latency is free
idea: MXT (2000) compressed all memory in 1 KB sectors behind a 32 MB L3, so every miss paid decompression and the extra cache chip cost more than the DRAM saved. Put an LZ4/zstd engine inside a CXL Type-3 expander that already costs ~150-250 ns, compress at 4 KB with a 64 MB uncompressed hot-line buffer, and expose 2-3x physical capacity as plain memory.
why: Cost per bit: 2-3x effective GB in the far tier; decompression hides inside the existing CXL hop, removing the latency and cost penalty that killed MXT.

title: Nantero NRAM, fixed: BEOL-only CNT fab hybrid-bonded to logic
idea: Nantero's carbon-nanotube NRAM stalled because fabs feared CNT contamination of front-end lines and integration took a decade. Fabricate the CNT switching layer in a dedicated BEOL-only fab on wafers carrying only select transistors, then hybrid-bond them to logic, so no mainline fab ever touches nanotubes.
why: A nonvolatile, refresh-free, capacitorless tier replacing part of DRAM, buildable in small, cheap U.S. BEOL fabs.

title: Canonicalized document KV shared across all tenants
idea: Inverts 'each request owns its KV cache': RAG chunks, tool schemas and system prompts are normalized into canonical position-independent KV blocks (re-rotated to the needed position at use) and stored once per cluster under a content hash, so any tenant that retrieves the same document reuses the same KV blocks.
why: In RAG and agent workloads 60-90% of context is shared documents, so KV memory per active user drops 5-20x.

title: Sub-page hardware meshing merges fragmented heap pages without moving objects
idea: Box: defragment × page-table extension × 1 KB chunk × background scan × chunk-mask PTE. A 4-bit chunk map in each PTE lets two virtual pages whose live 1 KB chunks do not overlap share one physical frame, so the allocator reclaims fragmentation while every pointer stays valid.
why: Fragmentation wastes 15–40% of RSS in long-running C/C++ services; hardware meshing recovers most of it, ~1.2–1.5× effective density.

title: Ice-cube tray: compressed lines carry size class inside freed ECC
idea: Each ice-tray slot has a fixed shape: compress every 64 B line into one of four slot classes, and when a line shrinks by at least 4 B write its 2-bit class and slot pointer into the freed bits alongside stronger ECC, so the controller never fetches a separate metadata table; incompressible lines use standard ECC with a flag symbol.
why: Metadata misses (10-30% latency penalty) are what kill hardware memory compression; embedding metadata makes 1.5-2x line compression viable at near-zero latency cost.

title: Erasure-coded in-memory stores replace triple replication
idea: TRIZ #34 Discarding and recovering: discard replicas and recover lost data from parity; in-memory caches and KV stores stripe objects RS(8,2) across servers' DRAM, with encode and decode done at line rate by a 180 nm XOR/Galois-field engine on the NIC.
why: 3x replication becomes 1.25x overhead, a ~58% DRAM saving for replicated in-memory datasets.

title: Pre-printed forms: frozen base weights, only adapters live in SRAM
idea: Borrowed from pre-printed forms where only the handwritten fields vary: models are split into a frozen base held in non-volatile storage and per-tenant low-rank adapters plus normalization deltas (a few MB each) held in on-die SRAM; the scheduler batches requests by adapter so mutable state never exceeds SRAM.
why: Multi-tenant fine-tune serving needs no DRAM for per-tenant weights and no refresh; 100+ tenants per accelerator instead of one full copy each.

title: Mars-rover precision on demand: bit-plane memory layout and tiering
idea: From rovers that downlink images progressively, most significant bits first: store tensors and images bit-plane-major, keep the top planes in DRAM and the low planes in flash or nowhere, and let each reader request only the planes its precision needs.
why: Many consumers (inference, previews, analytics) need 4-8 of 16-32 bits; plane tiering cuts DRAM 2-4x without fixing precision at write time.

title: Swap 3x in-memory replication for erasure-coded cache shards
idea: Substitute full replicas with parity. In-memory stores and caches split each object into k data shards plus m parity shards (e.g., 10+4) across nodes and read any k of them in parallel over RDMA. This is pure software on standard servers.
why: Fault-tolerance memory overhead drops from 3.0x to 1.4x, freeing ~50% of the DRAM in replicated cache tiers, and parallel reads cut tail latency.

title: Hashed compositional embeddings plus a learned head cache
idea: Combine the hashing trick (each ID composes its vector from several shared sub-tables via independent hashes) with a small table of fully learned rows for the hottest IDs; IDs are promoted to full rows as their frequency rises and demoted when they cool.
why: Recommendation models hold multi-TB embedding tables in DRAM; the long tail compresses 10-50x with little accuracy loss.

title: Sulfur vulcanization: cross-linked embedding tables from shared sub-vectors
idea: Vulcanization cross-links rubber chains with sulfur bridges; each row of a TB-scale recommendation embedding table is assembled from 4 shared sub-vectors picked from small pools by 4 independent hashes of the ID plus a 1-byte per-ID gain, and only frequent IDs are promoted to private rows.
why: Embedding tables are 90%+ of recommender model memory; cross-linking cuts them 10-50x with <0.1% accuracy loss on long-tail IDs (density, cost/bit).

title: Range-proven bit-precise fields with hardware bitfield load/store
idea: A field holding 0-100 needs 7 bits but is stored in 32 or 64. The compiler proves value ranges (abstract interpretation plus runtime guards) and packs struct fields at bit granularity; new bitfield load/store instructions with extract/insert at the memory side keep access single-cycle and trap on overflow so the layout can widen.
why: 20-40% smaller record-heavy data (in-memory databases, game state, ad features) with no change to algorithms.

title: Velcro: detachable memory chiplets outlive their accelerators
idea: Velcro lets parts be reused: attach LPDDR/HBM-class memory to accelerators with low-temperature anisotropic conductive film or fine-pitch sockets (<200 C) instead of permanent solder and underfill, so memory is harvested and redeployed when the compute die is replaced every 2-3 years.
why: Memory lasts 8-10 years while accelerators last 2-3; reuse multiplies effective supply ~2-3x over a decade.

title: Microheater-gated zirconia ionic memory hosts shared read-mostly pages
idea: Store deduplicated read-only pages (shared libraries, model weights, map tiles) in yttria-stabilized zirconia cells. Their oxygen-ion motion is frozen at 125 C but fast at ~400 C, so writes use a local microheater pulse and the hot ambient cannot disturb the data. Reads are fast and resistive.
why: Thermal write gating gives 10-year retention at 125 C, and one shared physical copy serves all processes and VMs, cutting DRAM 20-40%.

title: Tenants rent idle DRAM back to the provider every second
idea: Reverse ownership inside each server: VMs and containers hold memory as one-second leases priced by an auction in the hypervisor; tenants earn credits for memory they release, and the host hands it to memory-hungry neighbors through free-page reporting.
why: Cloud servers strand ~25% of DRAM; a market that pays tenants to release it can recover most of that, cutting fleet DRAM purchases 15-25%.

title: Two-layer DRAM window streams weights from parallel flash channels
idea: IFR: weights need no DRAM residency. Closest: weights live across 16-64 NVMe/low-latency flash channels and stream layer by layer into a double buffer holding exactly two layers; the batch grows until per-layer compute hides the flash read time.
why: Weight DRAM falls by L/2 (40-60x for 80-120-layer models) for offline inference and fine-tuning; flash costs ~1/20 per bit.

title: Self-describing paired lines with header-in-slack, no metadata table
idea: TRIZ #25 Self-service: when two adjacent 64 B lines each compress to 30 B or less, they are packed into one 64 B slot whose first bits describe the encoding, and the freed buddy slot goes to a free list; a decoder simple enough for 180 nm reads the header in-line, so no separate metadata table, metadata cache or extra DRAM access is needed.
why: Removes the metadata-access penalty that kills line compression; 1.3-1.8x capacity with decode logic small enough for old nodes.

title: Cesium clock TTL memory: allocations that expire in hardware
idea: Using a cesium-clock-style global timestamp, allocations made with a TTL (session state, request buffers, cache entries) carry an expiry field in line/page metadata, and the controller sweeps expired lines into a free list with no GC or free() call, faulting cleanly if a stale pointer touches them.
why: Services keep expired session and cache data for minutes to hours because sweeping is costly; hardware expiry trims resident memory 20-40% for TTL-heavy workloads (cost/bit).

title: Ant pheromone trails: refresh operations decay per-page hotness counters
idea: Ant trails fade unless re-walked: keep a 3-bit hotness counter per page in spare on-die ECC/metadata bits; accesses increment it and the DRAM's own refresh, which already opens every row, decrements it for free, giving the controller hardware-aged heat maps to drive tiering with zero sampling overhead.
why: Tiering accuracy limits how much DRAM cheaper tiers can replace; free precise hotness lets 30-50% of footprint leave DRAM versus ~15-20% with page-table scanning.

title: Resonant-tunneling diodes decompress memory lines inline at line rate
idea: Put a multi-valued logic block of InGaAs/AlAs resonant-tunneling diodes (negative differential resistance, 100+ GHz) on the memory channel. Every 64-byte line can then be stored compressed (base-delta or entropy-coded) and expanded within one memory clock. With no latency penalty, the OS has no reason to keep any data uncompressed.
why: Transparent compression gives 1.5-2x effective capacity across all memory, not just cold pages (fact 5).

title: Fettling attention: grind off flip burrs from KV before softmax
idea: Foundry fettling grinds the burrs off sand castings. The KV cache lives in 1%-BER cells as int4, with per-head scales protected. The attention kernel 'fettles' each key and value it loads by clamping it to calibrated per-channel bounds and capping softmax weights (top-k trimmed), so a flip that creates an outlier logit cannot hijack attention.
why: Moves the KV cache, the biggest inference memory consumer, to cheap low-refresh cells. int4 already gives 4x capacity, and robust aggregation is expected to keep perplexity within about 0.1-0.3 at 1% BER.

title: Swap server-side user state for client-carried signed state blobs
idea: Substitute server memory with the client's memory. Recommendation and session services stop keeping per-user embeddings, histories and sessions in DRAM: each client holds its own encrypted, signed state vector of a few KB and attaches it to every request, and servers keep only shared item tables.
why: Per-user tables reach terabytes per model on large platforms, and moving them to clients removes a large share of recommendation-serving DRAM.

title: Memory-in-pixel panels absorb the framebuffer out of DRAM
idea: A display backplane already is a memory: every pixel has a TFT and a storage capacitor on glass. Put a 1-3 bit latch or oxide-TFT gain cell in each subpixel (memory-in-pixel) and composite static layers directly in the panel, so phones, laptops and VR headsets stop keeping triple-buffered framebuffers and static layers in DRAM.
why: Frees 100-500 MB per device (4K-8K, multiple layers, triple buffering) plus the refresh traffic; small per device, but across billions of units.

title: Switch-SRAM hot tier ends per-server hot-key replication
idea: Worsen: replicate the hottest keys on every cache server to survive load skew. Flip: serve the top 0.1% of keys from the SRAM of programmable top-of-rack switches, which absorbs skew in-network, so servers stop keeping replicas and run at higher fill.
why: Capacity: 20-40% less DRAM in skewed key-value fleets, which are currently over-replicated for hot spots.

title: Vinyl pressing: frozen model weights stamped into via-programmed ROM
idea: Like pressing millions of records from one master, burn a released model's weights into via- or metal-programmed ROM chiplets (mature node, one custom mask, no EUV) bonded beside the accelerator; weights are inherently non-volatile and DRAM holds only KV and small LoRA patches.
why: ROM needs no capacitor or refresh and is several times denser than DRAM at mature nodes; removes weights from DRAM entirely and is U.S.-manufacturable on existing fabs.

title: Sun Rock scout threads, fixed: compiler helper threads hide far memory
idea: Sun's Rock used hardware 'scout' threads to run ahead and prefetch but was cancelled for power and complexity. Do it in software: the compiler emits a stripped address-generation slice that runs on an SMT sibling ahead of the main thread, prefetching from a slow CXL/NAND tier into cache so most data can live off-DRAM.
why: Lets 60-80% of capacity move to a 5-10x cheaper, 3-10x slower tier while hiding most of its latency for irregular code.

title: Memory futures market inside the cluster scheduler
idea: Borrow commodity futures: jobs buy forward contracts for GB-hours at submission, the scheduler clears the market every minute, and spot-price spikes automatically switch jobs into pre-registered compressed or recompute modes or let them sell capacity back.
why: Price signals reveal which jobs can shrink cheaply; claims 15-25% lower peak DRAM provisioning in shared AI clusters by flattening demand.

title: Factory seconds: sell test-reject DRAM dies as AI-grade memory
idea: Outlet stores sell slightly flawed 'seconds'. DRAM makers take dies that fail JEDEC retention or defect screens but run at about 1% raw BER under relaxed refresh, and bin them into an 'AI-grade' SKU: CXL modules with a page-level LDPC controller, sold for error-tolerant data such as KV, activations and low bit-planes.
why: Recovers the 5-15% of dies that are scrapped or down-binned and lets marginal process windows ship, adding usable bit supply without a new fab at a lower cost per GB.

title: Zebrafish-heart regeneration: spare die and reroutable TSVs in HBM
idea: Zebrafish regrow damaged heart muscle; each HBM stack carries one spare core die and redundant TSV lanes, and field logic bypasses a failing die and reroutes broken TSVs, so the stack is repaired in place instead of the whole accelerator being scrapped.
why: HBM TSV yield tax (20-30%) and field failures: fewer scrapped stacks and GPUs per usable GB.

title: Rewrite random-access algorithms as streaming passes over disk
idea: Worsen: write pointer-chasing code that demands everything in DRAM. Flip: recast graph, join and sort workloads as external-memory streaming algorithms (sort-merge, bucketed scatter-gather, semi-streaming graph sketches) so data lives on HDD or QLC and DRAM holds only sort buffers.
why: Cost: HDD at about $0.015/GB vs DRAM at $10+/GB, over 500x cheaper; trades algorithm redesign and wall-clock time.

title: Layer-major batching: one layer resident across thousands of requests
idea: Swap the serving loop nest from token-outer/layer-inner to layer-outer/request-inner: run layer L for a whole queue of thousands of requests, then evict it and load L+1 from flash or far memory, so DRAM holds only one layer's weights plus that layer's KV slice at a time.
why: For throughput-oriented offline inference, resident weights drop by the depth factor (~60-120x) and total DRAM need falls 5-20x, at the cost of latency.

title: Router lookahead predicts MoE experts for just-in-time paging
idea: Combine the mixture-of-experts gating network with a prefetcher: a cheap distilled copy of layer L+2's router runs on layer L's hidden state to predict which experts will fire, and those experts are paged from flash/CXL into HBM two layers ahead, so only ~10-20% of experts are resident.
why: MoE models leave 80-95% of weights inactive per token; DRAM for weights shrinks 5-10x.

title: Eliminate idle-expert residency with one-layer-ahead MoE expert prefetch
idea: An open-source MoE runtime runs the next layer's router on the current hidden state to predict its experts one layer early and streams them over PCIe from host or NVMe, so HBM holds only about 25% of experts plus a hot cache.
why: MoE models need 3-4x less accelerator memory, which directly reduces HBM, the scarcest DRAM product.

title: Double-cloth weaving: cross-node erasure code replaces replicas and ECC
idea: Double cloth interlaces two layers so either one can carry the load. In-memory stores that replicate 3x across servers instead protect pages with a product code. A light inner LDPC per node (about 6%) cleans most of each node's 1%-BER flips, and an outer (8+3) erasure code across 11 servers corrects whatever the inner decode misses as well as whole-node loss. Per-DIMM ECC goes away.
why: Replication overhead drops from 3x to about 1.45x (about 2x less DRAM), the local ECC tax disappears, and cheap 1%-BER modules become usable.

title: Hardware forwarding enables low-headroom pauseless compaction
idea: Worsen: give garbage-collected runtimes 2-3x heap headroom so the GC rarely runs. Flip: the memory controller holds forwarding tables and a read barrier, so objects relocate concurrently with no pauses and heaps can run at 1.2x of live data.
why: Capacity: 40-60% less DRAM for Java, Go, .NET and JavaScript fleets, which hold a large share of server memory.

title: Frequency-domain KV: DCT along sequence, drop high bands
idea: Rearrange the KV cache from time order to frequency order: blocks of 64 tokens are transformed per channel with a DCT along the sequence axis, high-frequency coefficients are quantized hard or dropped, and attention reads the inverse-transformed block.
why: KV channels change slowly across neighboring tokens, so 3-6x compression beyond token quantization is plausible, as a kernel on existing GPUs with no new silicon.

title: Minify fragmentation: hardware page meshing at line granularity
idea: Minify allocator fragmentation: the memory controller finds two sparsely filled physical pages whose live 64 B lines do not overlap and merges them into one frame. Both virtual pages keep pointing at it through a line-offset remap, so it works like the Mesh allocator but transparently and for every language.
why: Long-running servers lose 20-40% of RAM to fragmentation, and meshing reclaims most of it.

title: Line-granular copy-on-write for forks, snapshots and VM clones
idea: Box: share × MMU plus memory controller × 64 B line (not 4 KB page) × first write × per-page 64-bit diverged-line mask. Cloned pages keep pointing at the parent frame; a write copies only the touched line into a small overlay frame, and the controller merges parent and overlay on reads using the mask.
why: Serverless snapshots, VM clones and forked workers duplicate a full 4 KB page to change a few bytes; line CoW cuts post-fork memory growth 5–20×, packing more instances per GB.

title: Bit-plane tensor layout enables precision-on-demand memory
idea: Combine image bit-plane slicing with memory placement: store each BF16/FP8 tensor as separate pages per bit plane (sign+exponent, high mantissa, low mantissa). Low-significance planes are placed in compressed or slower tiers or dropped under pressure, and kernels fetch only the planes their current precision needs.
why: 25-50% of tensor bytes become optional, so memory pressure degrades precision gracefully instead of forcing OOM or swap.

title: Eliminate the stored KV cache: recompute K/V from residual checkpoints
idea: Instead of keeping K and V for every layer, store only the residual-stream vector every 8th layer per token and regenerate K/V for the intermediate layers on the fly during decode, using the FLOPs that sit idle in memory-bound decoding.
why: Attacks data movement and KV capacity: 4-8x less KV memory per session, turning a memory-bound phase into a compute-bound one on hardware with spare FLOPs.

title: Denning working-set billing for cloud memory
idea: Price cloud memory by each VM/container's measured working set (Denning 1968, sampled by WSClock in the hypervisor) instead of reserved GiB, auto-demoting untouched pages to compressed or far tiers and exposing the meter to developers.
why: Fleets typically touch 40-60% of allocated DRAM; a price signal on working set plus transparent demotion lets providers buy 25-40% less DRAM for the same customers.

title: RFID sweep: in-storage parallel scan replaces DRAM indexes
idea: Like an RFID reader inventorying a whole warehouse in one sweep instead of consulting a ledger, records in NV carry their own tags and computational-storage controllers scan all flash channels in parallel, using per-block Bloom summaries kept in the NV itself, eliminating DRAM-resident indexes.
why: Secondary indexes can rival data size in DRAM; 100+ GB/s internal flash bandwidth makes index-free lookup viable for many queries.

title: Minify precision on demand with bit-plane sliced storage
idea: Minify what stays resident by storing tensors, images and sensor arrays transposed into bit planes. The top planes live in DRAM and the low-order planes in CXL flash, which are fetched only when a consumer asks for full precision.
why: Many readers (previews, early training epochs, approximate queries) need only the top 4-8 bits, which gives ~1.5-3x less DRAM plus lower bandwidth.

title: Snapshot-and-restore replaces warm serverless sandbox pools
idea: Reverse 'keep warm' into 'keep cold, restore fast': idle function sandboxes are snapshotted to NVMe and restored in ~5-10 ms by lazily faulting in only the pages the first invocation touches, instead of holding thousands of warm VMs in DRAM.
why: Warm pools often leave 50-80% of serverless DRAM idle; replacing them cuts that DRAM 3-5x in software alone.

title: Dairy fresh-processing: consume activations in-DRAM before they decay
idea: Borrowed from dairies that process milk within hours rather than store it: activations are written into refresh-free DRAM subarrays and consumed within microseconds by charge-sharing multiply-accumulate in the same subarray (processing-in-memory), so no datum ever has to outlive milliseconds.
why: Combines compute-in-memory with ephemerality: zero refresh power, 3-20 pJ/bit of host data movement avoided, and capacitors sized for microseconds rather than 64 ms.

title: Reject-bin DRAM dies used for error-tolerant data classes
idea: Worsen: scrap every die with weak cells and demand perfection for all data. Flip: tag allocations by criticality and route error-tolerant classes (KV cache, gradients, video frames, caches) to cheap, partly failing dies that run with relaxed refresh, keeping pointers and code on perfect dies.
why: Supply and cost: uses 5-15% of output now discarded and lets lower-grade dies serve half the footprint.

title: Tailor's made-to-measure: compiler narrows struct fields to observed ranges
idea: A tailor cuts cloth to the body, not a standard size. An LLVM plugin profiles field value ranges in production and rewrites hot structs with bit-packed narrow fields (int64 to int20, enums to 3 bits, pointers to 32-bit indices). A cheap overflow check migrates an object to a wide spill layout if a value ever exceeds its range. Three compiler engineers can do it in 24 months.
why: Typical C++/Rust structs are 30-50% padding and over-wide fields, so this cuts the heap 20-35% on data-structure-heavy services.

title: Hydra stem-cell spare pool differentiates into failed modules
idea: Hydra renews itself from stem cells; each rack keeps 3-5% of memory as undifferentiated hot spares that silently mirror compressed copies of the most failure-prone ranges and instantly take over an address range, with dead units swapped in monthly batch maintenance.
why: Replaces per-server 10-20% headroom with rack-level 3-5% while letting fleets run aged modules.

title: Broadcast read bus killing per-bank data replication in PIM
idea: Processing-in-memory DIMMs replicate lookup tables and model parameters in every bank, because each PIM unit sees only its own bank. One added metal mask routes a die-wide broadcast read bus, so every PIM unit reads one shared copy at the moment it is fetched. Sharing moves from the bank scale to the die scale.
why: PIM replication of shared data (often 8-64x) falls to 1, freeing most PIM capacity for unique data.

title: Ripstop weave: error-contained compression for media and sensor buffers
idea: Ripstop fabric has a heavy thread every few mm so tears cannot spread. Compressed video frames, images and sensor streams kept in memory use fixed-length transform-coefficient codes and reversible variable-length codes, with a resync point every 32 symbols. A flip then corrupts one coefficient in one block instead of the rest of the stream, and the decoder conceals damaged blocks from their neighbors.
why: Camera, video-analytics and vehicle-log buffers can stay compressed 5-20x in 1%-BER memory instead of being decompressed into perfect DRAM.

title: Imaginal-disc HBM lifts off via pressure contacts for next boards
idea: Insect imaginal discs survive metamorphosis into the adult; HBM stacks mount to the interposer through anisotropic conductive film or micro-spring pressure contacts instead of permanent microbumps, so stacks can be lifted off a dead or obsolete accelerator and placed on its successor.
why: HBM supply and TSV-yield tax: one stack serves 2-3 accelerator generations.

title: Erasure-coded in-memory stores instead of full replicas
idea: Inverts 'durability in memory means 2-3 full replicas': in-memory databases and caches store data as k+m erasure-coded stripes across nodes (e.g., 4+2) and rebuild them over RDMA when a node fails.
why: Replica DRAM overhead falls from 100-200% to ~50%, about a 2x fleet DRAM saving for replicated stores.

title: Contact sheets: statistical sketches in DRAM, full records in NV
idea: Like photographers picking from thumbnails before pulling negatives, keep probabilistic sketches (count-min, HyperLogLog, quantile digests) in DRAM and full records in persistent memory; queries that tolerate bounded error are answered from sketches and only exact queries touch NV.
why: Sketches are 100-1000x smaller than raw data; analytics DRAM shrinks drastically while ground truth stays durable.

title: Photorefractive crystal associative memory prefilters attention keys
idea: Attention is a correlation search, and optics does correlation natively. Record the keys as holographic gratings in an iron-doped lithium-niobate crystal; a query beam diffracts into correlation peaks whose brightness ranks the keys, and only the top-k token positions are fetched from a compressed KV store for exact attention.
why: Full-precision KV no longer has to sit in fast DRAM, because only the top-k (<5%) is read. The KV store can then be compressed or tiered, ~10x less DRAM for million-token contexts.

title: Execute directly on compressed data, never decompress into DRAM
idea: Reverse decompress-then-compute: near-memory ALUs run filters, joins and aggregates directly on dictionary-, run-length- and bit-packed column encodings, and LLM kernels consume codebook-quantized weights as indices, so no decompressed copy is ever materialized in DRAM.
why: Removes transient decompressed buffers and keeps data at 3-10x compression throughout analytics and inference.

title: Memory rationing by merit: domestic DRAM goes to efficient workloads
idea: Po: memory is rationed like wartime sugar. Under Defense Production Act priority authority, domestic DRAM output and federal cloud memory go first to workloads certified on a public bytes-per-unit-work benchmark (GB per 1k inferences, per query), with tiers reset yearly.
why: Turns scarce U.S.-made supply into an efficiency incentive: vendors cut footprint to get supply, compounding 10-30% savings across federal and defense computing.

title: Kanban cards for layer streaming from SSD to GPU
idea: Toyota-style kanban: a hardware credit counter between the GPU and an NVMe controller releases the next layer's weights or KV pages only when a consumer slot frees, so DRAM/HBM holds exactly pipeline-depth (2-3 layers) of inventory, never the whole model.
why: Runs models 5-10x larger than HBM at near-full batch throughput; substitutes cheap flash bandwidth for DRAM capacity.

title: HPE memristor, fixed: stochastic switching as probabilistic optimizer counters
idea: HPE's memristor died because its stochastic, variable switching made it unreliable storage. Turn the flaw into the feature: store Adam moments as Morris-style probabilistic counters in memristor crossbars, where each pulse switches a cell with a known probability, giving unbiased stochastic rounding for free.
why: Optimizer state (8-12 B/param) dominates training memory; ~1 B/param probabilistic counters cut it ~8x with no capacitor and no DRAM.

title: Brood-to-honey comb reuse time-multiplexes training buffers
idea: Bee comb cells switch from rearing brood to storing honey; the compiler likewise assigns each physical DRAM region a planned succession of roles (forward activation, then gradient, then optimizer scratch) from a global lifetime graph with in-place kernels, so no region idles between roles.
why: Training peak memory: 25-40% lower peak footprint per accelerator.

title: Audio mastering dither: retention decay as free training noise
idea: Borrowed from audio mastering, where deliberate dither noise improves perceived quality: activations saved for backprop live in refresh-free DRAM, with sign/exponent bits stored in the non-leaking state so only mantissa LSBs can decay, and the sparse bit flips that accrue before the backward pass act as stochastic-rounding/dropout-like noise.
why: Zero refresh for training's largest memory consumer, and decay tolerance admits denser weak-retention cells; could be accuracy-neutral or even regularizing.

title: Fairchild CCD serial memory revived as sequential weight streamer
idea: Revive 1975 CCD serial memories (serial-parallel-serial organization): a double-poly CCD chip built at 0.5-1 um in a university nanofab holds weights as charge packets that shift past one output amplifier per register in exactly the order inference reads them every token. Circulation regenerates charge, so there is no refresh controller, row decoder or storage capacitor.
why: Weights are read strictly sequentially, so random access is wasted; CCD needs ~2-4F^2 and no capacitor or contact per bit, a periphery-free (fact 7) weight tier that takes weights out of DRAM, demonstrated in a university fab and then moved to any image-sensor fab.

title: Nickel foam meshing: hardware merges sparse pages with disjoint objects
idea: Like open-cell nickel foam, many heap pages are mostly holes; a background engine finds page pairs whose live 64 B lines do not overlap, copies one into the other's holes, and maps both virtual pages to one physical frame via a line mask in a TLB extension, so no pointers or virtual addresses change.
why: Mesh-style compaction for unmanaged C/C++ heaps recovers 15-40% of fragmented memory without pointer updates (density, cost/bit).

title: LEGO kit-of-parts: compositional embeddings from small shared brick tables
idea: LEGO builds endless models from a few brick types. Terabyte-scale recommendation embedding tables are replaced by compositional embeddings: each ID's vector is the sum of 4 vectors drawn from small 'brick' tables indexed by a hash or quotient-remainder split of the ID. A flip in one brick contributes only a quarter of the vector's error, and the bricks are trained with 1% flip injection.
why: Recommendation embeddings are among the largest DRAM users (multi-TB per model); compositional tables shrink them 10-1000x and tolerate 1% BER by construction.

title: Matryoshka weight residency: MSB nest in DRAM, residual off-board
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting: quantize weights with nested codebooks so the 4-bit code is literally the top nibble of the 8-bit code; DRAM/HBM holds only the 4-bit nest while the residual nibble sits in CXL memory or flash and is streamed per layer only when a cheap per-token confidence probe says that layer needs full precision.
why: Halves weight memory in the common case while keeping an INT8 quality ceiling; 1.6-2x capacity for weight-bound inference.

title: Keep 2-byte token IDs, re-encode middle-context KV on demand
idea: Worsen: hold about 100 KB of KV per token for the whole context. Flip: evict KV for middle context, keep only the token IDs, and when a light attention predictor flags a region as relevant, recompute that region's KV in a batched prefill burst.
why: Capacity: up to 1000x less storage per evicted token; trades extra compute (cheap) for HBM (scarce).

title: Host-DRAM-lite AI servers decode data shards directly on GPU
idea: IFR: AI-server host memory shrinks to almost nothing. Constraint: adding no new chips means adding no scarce elements, so delete host DRAM's jobs instead: compressed training shards go storage-to-GPU and are decoded by GPU kernels, and checkpoints stream GPU-to-NVMe directly, removing the staging buffers that justify 1-2 TB per node.
why: Host DRAM per AI node drops from ~2 TB to ~256 GB, an 8x cut on a large slice of server DRAM bought today.

title: SPC control charts per row: data classes follow measured cell quality
idea: Statistical process control tracks each machine against control limits. The memory controller keeps a CUSUM chart of corrected and detected errors for every row (from scrub and parity) and classifies rows as A (<0.01%), B (<0.3%) or C (up to 1%). Pages are remapped so precise data lives in A rows, approximate tensors in B rows, and noise-tolerant data (KV tails, activation stash, low bit-planes) in C rows.
why: Cell quality varies about 100x across a die; matching data tolerance to measured row quality lets whole modules run at relaxed refresh or voltage with 1% worst-case rows instead of paying for guard bands.

title: Superword tokenizer halves tokens and halves KV per conversation
idea: IFR: a whole thought fits in one KV slot. Closest with no hardware: retrain tokenizers with ~1M-entry multi-word vocabularies (frequent phrases as single tokens), moving cost into a larger embedding table that is stored once while every live sequence carries ~2x fewer tokens.
why: KV memory scales with token count; ~40-50% KV cut fleet-wide for a one-time embedding cost.

title: Foveated KV precision falls off with attention eccentricity
idea: Like the retina's dense fovea and sparse periphery, each attention head stores KV at 8-bit for the top-attended 5% of tokens, 4-bit for the next band and 1-2-bit sketches for the periphery; a 'saccade' (attention shift onto a peripheral token) re-fetches its full-precision copy from a compressed backing tier.
why: KV capacity and bandwidth: 3-5x fewer bits per token at near-baseline quality.

title: Chameleon skin: lines change encoding instead of location
idea: A chameleon changes colour, not position: rather than migrating cold pages to another device, the controller re-encodes them in place (raw, then light base-delta, then heavy dictionary/entropy) as they cool and returns the slack to a common pool; hot accesses promote them back to raw.
why: Delivers tiering's capacity benefit without a second memory device or link; 1.3-2x effective capacity in the same DIMMs.
